title: Bakery deliveries
topic: A shop owner compares rainy-day and dry-day late deliveries without total rain counts
blurb: A friend who runs a bakery is reviewing recent late delivery tickets.
prompt: A friend just sent this in the group chat. Tap a line if something doesn't add up, or let it pass.

segments.label: The batch
segments.text: Pulled our bakery's last 300 local deliveries to see where late orders are coming from.

segments.label: The counts
segments.text: 42 of those 300 orders were rainy-day and late; 14 were dry-day and late.

segments.label: The ratio
segments.text: So grab any late ticket from that pile and it's 3× as likely to be a rain day as a dry day — doesn't even matter how often it rained.

segments.label: The plan
segments.text: Three-quarters of our late tickets sit on rain days, so I'm auditing rainy-day routes first.

conclusion: A random late order from that batch is 3× as likely to be from a rainy day, regardless of how often it rained.

diagnosis: 300 deliveries is too small a slice unless it spans a full year of dry and wet seasons.
Only checking local deliveries ignores pickup delays that might share the same kitchen bottleneck.
You can't compare weather effects without splitting the 300 orders into equal rainy and dry halves first.
A single bakery's last 300 orders won't separate courier traffic from kitchen prep delays.
fix: Pull a full 12 months of deliveries so rainy and dry seasons balance out.
Include in-store pickup orders before diagnosing where delays happen.
Sample 150 rainy-day orders and 150 dry-day orders before comparing counts.
Split kitchen prep time from road time before counting late tickets.

diagnosis: 42 and 14 are raw counts out of 300, not percentages of rainy vs dry orders, so you can't compare them yet.
56 late orders out of 300 is 18.7%, which leaves out the 244 on-time orders you need for the real ratio.
Without knowing how many of the 300 orders happened in the rain, 42 vs 14 tells you nothing.
Listing only late orders hides whether dry days had way fewer total deliveries.
fix: Divide 42 by total rainy-day orders and 14 by total dry-day orders first.
Report the 244 on-time deliveries split by weather before taking any ratio.
Convert 42/300 (14%) and 14/300 (4.7%) into per-weather lateness rates.
Throw out the 300 denominator and compare only orders from the same weekday.

diagnosis: You're missing the rainy-day share: if 250 of the 300 orders happened in the rain, rainy orders aren't 3× more likely to be late at all.
Dividing 42 by 14 ignores the 244 on-time orders, so the true ratio can't be 3-to-1.
Whether it rained 20 days or 2 days completely changes the conditional odds, so saying it doesn't matter is backwards.
42 out of 56 is 75%, which is 50 percentage points higher than 25%, not three times higher.
fix: Check how many total rainy vs dry orders were in the 300 before quoting a 3× ratio.
Compute P(late | rain) divided by P(late | dry) instead of dividing 42 by 14.
Drop the claim that rainy-day frequency doesn't matter — it sits right in the denominator.
State it as 14% vs 4.7% of all 300 orders instead of a 3× conditional chance.

diagnosis: Auditing rainy-day routing first only makes sense if rain actually raises the per-order lateness rate.
42 out of 300 is only 14%, not three-quarters — you mixed up the denominator between 56 and 300.
Admitting it might just be a wet month undercuts line 3's claim that rain makes late orders 3× as likely.
If most orders happened on rainy days, fixing dry-day routing could actually save more orders.
fix: Wait until you verify rainy orders are late at a higher rate before changing rain routing.
Change 'three-quarters' to 14% so it matches 42 out of 300.
Audit dry-day and rainy-day routes equally until you know total rainy-day volume.
Check whether the dry-day late rate is actually higher per delivery first.

clean_segments: Pulled our bakery's last 300 local deliveries to see where late orders are coming from.
42 of those 300 orders were rainy-day and late; 14 were dry-day and late.
So grab any late ticket from that pile and it's 3× as likely to be a rain day as a dry day — doesn't even matter how often it rained.
Three-quarters of our late tickets sit on rain days, so I'm auditing rainy-day routes first.
clean_conclusion: How often it rained only matters if you ask whether rain *causes* lateness. Here they asked the reverse — grab one of the 56 late tickets, and 42/56 vs 14/56 really is 3-to-1.
explanation: How often it rained only matters if you ask whether rain *causes* lateness. Here they asked the reverse — grab one of the 56 late tickets, and 42/56 vs 14/56 really is 3-to-1.
